objects.title: Multi-format file ingestion
objects.proves: The platform natively ingests five file formats with real-world “gotchas”: CSV with quoted/embedded delimiters, pipe-delimited text, multi-sheet Excel (targeting a named sheet), nested JSON, and XML with optional nodes.
objects.setup: Foundation source files are staged on the landing Volume. Pre-built notebook deployed to /Workspace/Shared/Princeton POC/1 - Engineer/E1 - Multi-format file ingestion.
steps: In the Databricks Assistant (sparkle panel), enter the prompt below.
Genie generates the ingestion pipeline; run it.
Check the expected outcome — five bronze tables in your schema.
objects.prompt:
I'm building a Lakeflow Spark Declarative Pipeline (Python) that ingests five higher-ed source files into bronze streaming tables using Auto Loader. Write the pipeline for me.

Important: each source is staged in its OWN directory under /Volumes/princeton_poc_dev/landing_dev/files/ — Auto Loader reads a directory, not a single file — so point each streaming table at the directory. Create one @dp.table streaming table per source, reading with spark.readStream.format("cloudFiles"), and let Auto Loader manage its own schema location and checkpoints (don't set them). Enable cloudFiles.inferColumnTypes on each.

Create these five tables in catalog princeton_poc_dev, schema wksp_<my_user>:

1. e1_students_raw — dir students_csv/ — cloudFiles.format csv, header true, quote '"', escape '"' (a name field contains an embedded comma inside quotes; it must stay one field).
2. e1_enrollments_raw — dir enrollments_pipe/ — cloudFiles.format csv, header true, sep "|".
3. e1_financial_aid_raw — dir financial_aid_xlsx/ — cloudFiles.format excel, dataAddress "AidDetail" (read only that named sheet, not the first), headerRows 1. Excel via Auto Loader does NOT support schema evolution, so set cloudFiles.schemaEvolutionMode "none".
4. e1_course_catalog_raw — dir course_catalog_json/ — cloudFiles.format json, multiLine true (nested objects/arrays).
5. e1_faculty_raw — dir faculty_xml/ — cloudFiles.format xml, rowTag "faculty" (optional <tenure> node should come through as null, not drop the row).

The pipeline's target catalog + schema are set in the pipeline settings, so reference each table by its short name; don't hard-code the catalog inside the code.
objects.outcome: Five tables in your per-person wksp_<you> schema — e1_students_raw (2000), e1_enrollments_raw (2000), e1_financial_aid_raw (1000, from the AidDetail sheet only), e1_course_catalog_raw (10 depts), e1_faculty_raw (200). The row "Doe, John" proves the embedded comma didn't split (SE-04); the ~66/134 tenure-present/null split proves the optional XML node became null, not a dropped row (SE-07).
notes: Native Excel read works (DBR 17.1+) via .option("dataAddress", "AidDetail") — a bare sheet name.
Outputs go to a per-person schema (wksp_<current_user>) so ~20 people run it concurrently without colliding; the foundation stays read-only.

objects.title: REST API ingestion — OAuth 2.0 + pagination + token refresh
objects.proves: The platform ingests from a paginated REST API using OAuth 2.0 client-credentials, following pagination automatically and refreshing the token on expiry — with no manual intervention.
objects.setup: Mock API app princeton-mock-api is deployed and running; a service principal with CAN_USE on the app; its OAuth secret stored in UC secret scope princeton_poc_e3. Before running, confirm the app is up: databricks apps get princeton-mock-api should show RUNNING.
steps: In the Databricks Assistant (sparkle panel), enter the prompt below (replace <workspace-host> with your workspace URL).
Genie generates the ingestion notebook; run it.
Check the expected outcome — 60,000 rows with an automatic token refresh.
objects.prompt:
Write a notebook that ingests a paginated REST API served by the Databricks App named "princeton-mock-api", which sits behind the Databricks Apps SSO proxy. Get the app's base URL from `databricks apps get princeton-mock-api` (the "url" field), e.g. https://princeton-mock-api-<id>.<region>.databricksapps.com.

There are TWO SEPARATE sets of credentials — do not mix them up:
  • Layer-1 (Apps SSO proxy): a SERVICE PRINCIPAL's client_id/client_secret, read from secret scope princeton_poc_e3. Used only to get a workspace OAuth token.
  • Layer-2 (the app's own OAuth): the app's OWN demo credentials, which are literally client_id="princeton_poc_client" and client_secret="poc_secret_change_me" (these are the app's fixed demo creds, NOT the service principal's — pass them as literals).

Steps:
  1. POST https://<workspace-host>/oidc/v1/token with grant_type=client_credentials, scope=all-apis, using the SP client_id/client_secret from scope princeton_poc_e3. Take the returned access_token — call it PLATFORM_TOKEN.
  2. POST {base_url}/oauth/token with grant_type=client_credentials and the APP's demo client_id/client_secret ("princeton_poc_client" / "poc_secret_change_me"), AND send header Authorization: Bearer PLATFORM_TOKEN (so the call clears the SSO proxy). Take the returned access_token — call it API_TOKEN.
  3. GET {base_url}/enrollments with BOTH headers on every request:
       Authorization: Bearer PLATFORM_TOKEN
       X-API-Token: API_TOKEN            <-- the RAW token, NOT "Bearer <token>"
     Pagination is PAGE-NUMBER based: send params page (start at 1) and page_size=1000. The JSON response has fields total, data (the rows), and next (the next page NUMBER, or null when done). Loop until next is null. On HTTP 401, re-run step 2 to refresh API_TOKEN and retry the same page. Use page_size=1000 (the API's max) so it's ~60 pages, not 600.
Write all rows to catalog princeton_poc_dev, schema wksp_<my_user>, table e3_enrollments_from_api. Add a request timeout on every call. Assert the final row count equals the API's reported total. Never hardcode the SP secret (only the app's demo creds are literals).
objects.outcome: 60,000 rows in wksp_<you>.e3_enrollments_from_api; ~600 pages; a token refresh occurs mid-run (300s TTL) with no manual step; final count == API total.
notes: The SP + CAN_USE + secret-scope setup is a workspace-admin one-time task — also the answer to “how does an in-workspace pipeline call a gateway-protected internal API,” and doubles as PA-06 evidence.
SP credentials live only in the UC secret scope, never in notebook code.

objects.title: “Kitchen-sink” transformation pipeline
objects.proves: Ten transformation capabilities in one pipeline — the platform's breadth for real ETL work: lookups, joins, string/date/null handling, cast validation with reject paths, running totals, pivots, last-record-in-group, and a grouped summary.
objects.setup: Reads from princeton_poc_dev.silver_dev. Pre-built notebook deployed to /Workspace/Shared/Princeton POC/1 - Engineer/E5 - Transformation kitchen-sink.
steps: In the Databricks Assistant (sparkle panel), enter the prompt below.
Genie generates the transformation pipeline; run it.
Check the expected outcome — the ten transform patterns and the reject path.
objects.prompt:
Generate a Lakeflow Spark Declarative Pipeline reading from princeton_poc_dev.silver_dev, writing materialized views to catalog princeton_poc_dev, schema wksp_<my_user>, that demonstrates:
  - reference lookup enrichment with matched/unmatched handling
  - inner, left, and full outer joins
  - string manipulation (substring, concat, split, case)
  - null + conditional logic (coalesce, if/then/else)
  - parsing mixed-format date strings (use try_to_date / try_cast so bad values don't throw), extracting date parts, calculating date differences, AND converting a timestamp between time zones (the source is date-only, so stamp a UTC load timestamp and convert it to US/Eastern and US/Pacific with from_utc_timestamp)
  - casting with a reject path: use an expectation (expect_or_drop) to drop bad casts into the valid MV, and a separate MV that captures the rejected rows
  - running totals per group (control-break)
  - a pivot
  - last-record-per-group
  - a one-row-per-student summary
Name the lookup-enriched, one-row-per-student materialized view exactly `e5_student_enriched`, and give it a `standing` column derived from the student status (e.g. CASE WHEN status = 'graduated' THEN 'Alumnus' ELSE 'Active' END). Downstream steps (E7 target loading) read `e5_student_enriched` and filter on `standing`, so this name and column are a fixed contract even though the other MV names are free.
objects.outcome: Materialized views in wksp_<you>: e5_student_enriched (30000) with a standing column, e5_gpa_valid (~59988, bad casts dropped by the expectation), e5_gpa_rejects (the captured rejects, proving SE-16's reject path), running totals, a pivot, last-record-per-group, and a summary.
notes: The prompt is deliberately language-agnostic — Genie may generate SQL or Python, and may split the work into a different number of MVs. Both are first-class SDP; what matters is that all ten patterns are covered.
The reject path is a declarative Expectation (@dp.expect_or_drop) — valid rows flow through with drop-metrics tracked automatically; a sibling MV captures the rejects.
try_to_date / try_cast (not to_date/cast, which throw in ANSI mode) parse the mixed-format dates and tolerate bad casts.

objects.title: Change data capture + Slowly Changing Dimensions
objects.proves: Change-data-capture (new/changed/deleted) and both slowly-changing-dimension types, inferred automatically by diffing two snapshots — no hand-written CDC logic.
objects.setup: Run the E6 - snapshot setup notebook first — it builds student_snapshot_v1 (baseline) and student_snapshot_v2 (baseline + planted 10 inserts / 20 updates / 5 deletes) in your wksp schema. Then run the E6 pipeline.
steps: In the Databricks Assistant (sparkle panel), enter the prompt below.
Genie generates the CDC/SCD pipeline; run it. (The two snapshots it reads are pre-staged for you — see Setup.)
Check the expected outcome — SCD Type 1 and Type 2 tables.
objects.prompt:
Generate a Lakeflow SDP (Python) that uses apply_changes_from_snapshot to compare two student snapshots and infer inserts/updates/deletes. Feed the snapshots via a callable that returns wksp_<my_user>.student_snapshot_v1 as version 1, then wksp_<my_user>.student_snapshot_v2 as version 2, then None. keys = student_id. Build both:
  - e6_student_scd1 : SCD Type 1 (latest state / overwrite)
  - e6_student_scd2 : SCD Type 2 (full history with __START_AT / __END_AT)
Write to catalog princeton_poc_dev, schema wksp_<my_user>.
objects.outcome: e6_student_scd1 = 1005 (1000 − 5 deletes + 10 inserts); e6_student_scd2 = 1005 current + ~21 end-dated history rows. The known counts are the proof (SE-03/23 = detected changes; SE-21 = overwrite; SE-22 = history).
notes: The snapshot-diff is isolation-safe — it writes to your wksp and never mutates the shared silver_dev foundation, so a concurrent group session is safe.

objects.title: Target loading — UPSERT + multi-format export
objects.proves: Loading a database target with UPSERT + hard-delete, and exporting to CSV / pipe / Excel / JSON.
objects.setup: Requires E5's e5_student_enriched MV in your wksp schema. Pre-built notebook deployed to /Workspace/Shared/Princeton POC/1 - Engineer/E7 - Target loading.
steps: In the Databricks Assistant (sparkle panel), enter the prompt below.
Genie generates the target-loading notebook; run it.
Check the expected outcome — UPSERT result plus four export files.
objects.prompt:
Write a notebook that, using catalog princeton_poc_dev and schema wksp_<my_user>:
  1. Seeds a target table e7_student_target from a 500-row subset of e5_student_enriched.
  2. MERGEs the full e5_student_enriched into e7_student_target on student_id (update matched, insert unmatched) — an UPSERT.
  3. Hard-deletes alumni rows (standing = 'Alumnus') from the target.
  4. Exports the target to CSV, pipe-delimited, JSON, and Excel under /Volumes/princeton_poc_dev/landing_dev/files/e7_exports/wksp_<my_user>/.
Use native writers for CSV/pipe/JSON; write Excel with openpyxl in-memory.
objects.outcome: e7_student_target after UPSERT+delete (0 alumni remain, ~23,999 rows); four export artifacts under …/files/e7_exports/wksp_<you>/ (CSV, pipe, JSON, .xlsx).
notes: A notebook (not SDP) is the honest fit: SE-24's UPSERT + hard-delete needs a batch MERGE + DELETE, and pipeline sinks are streaming/append-only with no CSV/JSON/Excel option. Excel write uses openpyxl in-memory.

objects.title: Orchestration

steps: In the Databricks Assistant (sparkle panel), enter the prompt below.
Genie creates the serverless notebooks and wires the 7-task job; run it.
Check the expected outcome — each orchestration scenario proven per task.
objects.prompt:
Create a job with 7 tasks: a stage task, two parallel legs that both depend only on stage, a merge that depends on both legs, an external-command task, on the stage task enable "retry-enabled" task that simulates a transient failure, and a notification task, a paused daily cron schedule and job-level email notifications on success, on failure, AND on an SLA / duration breach (add a health rule on run duration so a run that exceeds the expected time triggers a duration-warning email).

create simple notebooks that execute on serverless for the tasks so the job can run. Make sure notebooks execute before adding to the job and fix any errors.
objects.outcome: Job TERMINATED SUCCESS. SE-28 chaining (dependency order) · SE-29 parallel (leg_a & leg_b overlap) · SE-30 retry (attempt 0 FAILED, attempt 1 SUCCESS) · SE-31 email notifications · SE-32 external command (subprocess) · SE-33 paused daily cron · SE-35 bulk pause from the Jobs UI.
notes: Two things make this generation actually run: the retry is enabled on the stage task (a concrete task to attach the transient-failure sim to), and the explicit “create serverless notebooks … make sure they execute before adding … fix any errors” instruction.
The retry demo is an honest transient-failure simulation keyed to the run id — it really fails once and recovers on retry.

objects.title: Bulk disable / pause of workloads
objects.proves: The platform can suspend every scheduled Engineer workload in one operation (a maintenance window) and re-enable them afterward — the fleet-wide control SE-31 asks for, distinct from pausing a single job's schedule.
objects.setup: Notebook engineer/src/e8/e8_bulk_pause.py is deployed with the bundle and uses the Jobs API (auto-authenticated on serverless — no extra credentials).
steps: Open the E8 - bulk pause notebook.
Set the action widget to "pause" and Run all — it lists every scheduled Engineer job, pauses each in one pass, and prints a before/after count.
Re-run with action = "resume" to restore every schedule.
Data Scientist, Business Analyst, and Platform-Admin jobs are excluded by the name filter — Engineer workloads only.
objects.outcome: All matched scheduled Engineer jobs flip to PAUSED in a single run (verified: 3 scheduled → 0 unpaused); no jobs fire during the window; resume restores them. The printed before/after counts are the proof.
notes: Scope is Engineer-only by design — the filter matches an (E#) or (SE-#) tag in the job name, so DS/BA/PA schedules are never touched.
Idempotent — only updates jobs whose schedule is in the opposite state, so re-running is safe.
The honest native answer to 'pause everything': Databricks has no single-button fleet pause, and an admin script over the Jobs API is exactly how a platform admin runs a maintenance window.

objects.title: DevOps — source control, promotion, CI/CD, rollback
objects.proves: The POC is engineered the way a production data platform is — versioned in Git, promoted across environments from one codebase, deployed by CI, and rollback-able. The repo + bundle + workflow are the deliverable; there's no notebook to run.
objects.setup: The repo, three bundle targets (dev/qa/prod, all validating), the CI workflow (.github/workflows/deploy.yml), and a known-good release tag.
steps: git log --oneline | head   — SE-36: versioned history, one commit per object
databricks bundle validate -t dev  --profile princeton_poc   — SE-37: same code…
databricks bundle validate -t qa   --profile princeton_poc   — …three catalogs
databricks bundle validate -t prod --profile princeton_poc
git tag   — SE-39: a known-good tag to roll back to
Open the repo's Actions tab — SE-38: the validate job runs on every push/PR; deploy is a manual dispatch.
objects.outcome: git log shows the versioned build history; all three bundle validate calls return Validation OK! (same code, princeton_poc_dev / _test / princeton_poc); git tag lists the release tag; the Actions tab shows the CI runs. Rollback = git revert or deploy a prior tag, then bundle deploy.
notes: Catalogs use UC default storage, so no storage_root / external location is needed per target (serverless workspaces).
The validate CI job catches configuration regressions before they reach an environment.

objects.setup: No build needed — lineage and Delta history are already populated by the POC's own pipeline/job runs.
steps: SE-40 lineage: run the table_lineage query below — returns real Bronze→Silver→Gold→wksp chains.

SE-43 AI docs: Catalog Explorer → silver_dev.student → AI suggest a description + column comments, then search to discover them.

steps: Run the PA-B task/notebook (or paste the shared masking prompt below).
Three graduated treatments: ssn partial (***-**-6789), dob generalised (1995-XX-XX), amount rounded to 1,000.
Admin sees full values (correct) — the role contrast is shown in PA-11's harness.
objects.prompt: Write a PySpark notebook that applies Unity Catalog column masks to sensitive columns and proves they work. Read widgets "catalog"/"schema_suffix" (concatenate directly). Target <catalog>.admin_demo ONLY — never silver/gold (SET MASK mutates the table object). Name every function with a _prompt suffix and attach nothing to a table that already has a policy (pre-built masks are live; SET MASK REPLACES). Use is_member('<group>'), NOT is_account_group_member() (admin=dbx_demo_shared_admins, faculty=data_engineers_demo_group). 1. Capture unmasked values first. 2. Three graduated masks: mask_ssn (full/admin, ***-**-last4/faculty, NULL else — NULL not '[REDACTED]'), mask_dob (year-only for faculty; dob is a STRING in 3 formats so coalesce over try_to_date), mask_amount (round(amount,-3) for faculty). 3. Attach with ALTER TABLE t ALTER COLUMN c SET MASK fn (that exact form; DROP MASK first for re-runnability) on student.ssn, student.dob, faculty.ssn, financial_aid.amount. 4. Re-query. 5. Assert admin view UNCHANGED, masks attached per information_schema.column_masks, zero NULL dob, and the shared foundation carries no policies.
objects.outcome: 3 mask functions, 4 columns masked on admin_demo; admin full, faculty partial, others NULL; dob parsed across all 3 formats; foundation carries no policies.
notes: The dob trap: dob is a STRING in 3 formats; year(dob) is NULL on two, so the mask coalesces try_to_date over all three. An assertion fails on any NULL dob.

objects.proves: Restriction is distinct from masking — for any role outside admin/faculty the mask returns NULL, not a '[REDACTED]' placeholder.
objects.setup: The third branch of each PA-B mask function.
steps: Run the PA-B notebook.
Read a restricted column as an unprivileged role → NULL for every row.

objects.title: Row-level security: attribute-based filtering
objects.proves: The same table returns different rows to different readers, enforced at the table rather than in a WHERE clause someone can forget.
objects.setup: PA-C task on admin_demo; a dept_id row filter.
steps: Run the PA-C notebook (or paste the shared row-filter prompt below).
Show 30,000 rows → a per-identity subset.
objects.prompt: Write a PySpark notebook that applies Unity Catalog row-level security with a policy driven by a lookup table rather than hardcoded values. Read widgets "catalog"/"schema_suffix" (concatenate directly). Target admin_demo only; _prompt-suffix your functions. Build a department_access mapping table keyed on current_user(); a row-filter function checks membership against it. Attach with ALTER TABLE t SET ROW FILTER fn ON (dept_id). Seed the running admin to two departments, show the filtered row count, then INSERT one row and show the visible set widen with NO policy change (that INSERT is the PA-10 demo). Assert: admin unrestricted; mapped identity sees a strict subset; unmapped principals see ZERO rows (deny by default); foundation clean.
objects.outcome: Admin unrestricted (30,000 rows); a mapped identity sees ~1,000 rows in 2 departments; unmapped principals see 0 rows (deny by default).
notes: Masks + filters compose — a faculty reader sees fewer rows AND masked columns within them.

objects.title: Row-level security: dynamic policy by user identity
objects.proves: The filter reads a department_access lookup keyed on current_user() — so a move is an INSERT, not a code change and redeploy.
objects.setup: Same PA-C notebook.
steps: Run the PA-C notebook.
It seeds the admin to two departments, shows the count, then INSERTs one row and shows the visible set widen — with NO policy edit.
That INSERT is the demonstration.

Build a department_access mapping table keyed on current_user(); a row-filter function checks membership against it. Attach with ALTER TABLE t SET ROW FILTER fn ON (dept_id). notes: Deny by default: an unmapped principal sees ZERO rows, not everything — asserted, because 'fails open' is the classic row-filter bug.

objects.title: Security policy testing & validation ("faux user")
objects.proves: A policy can be tested before rollout. Databricks has NO impersonation function, so the honest mechanisms are a test-twin function (proves the branches) and a second real principal (proves enforcement).
objects.setup: PA-D task; a test_mask_ssn_as(ssn, role) twin with role as an argument.
steps: Run the PA-D notebook.
Show the twin returns three distinct treatments of the same value (full / partial / NULL) and three row counts (all / subset / zero).
For enforcement proof: a colleague in the faculty group runs the query; the audit trail records their read.
objects.outcome: Three distinct treatments (full for admin, ***-**-6789 for faculty, NULL otherwise) + three row counts. The twin is named test_ and dropped so the inventory can't mistake it for a live policy.
notes: No impersonation fn exists (simulate_principal/set_session_user/impersonate all UNRESOLVED_ROUTINE). The twin proves the branch logic; claiming it proves ENFORCEMENT would overstate — say so in the read-out.

objects.title: Security policy audit & documentation
objects.proves: The policy catalog is a table you can query, not a console screen you screenshot — an access review is repeatable and cannot miss a table.
objects.setup: PA-D task; queries over information_schema.column_masks + row_filters.
steps: Run the PA-D notebook, or src/pa_d_policy_inventory.sql.
Show the inventory: 4 masks + 2 row filters, all in admin_demo.
Run the coverage-gap query — sensitive columns with NO policy, via a LEFT JOIN from information_schema.columns.
objects.outcome: 4 masks (student.ssn/dob, faculty.ssn, financial_aid.amount) + 2 row filters (student, faculty), all scoped to admin_demo; the coverage-gap check flags unprotected columns.
notes: The query worth showing is the coverage gap, not the inventory — the usual failure in a governed estate is an unprotected table nobody inventoried.

objects.title: Scale compute up / down (manual)
objects.proves: An administrator manually increases compute capacity for a heavy workload, then scales it back down — without interrupting active workloads.
objects.setup: A classic/pro SQL warehouse (manual scaling is a classic/pro operation; serverless auto-manages size).
steps: Execute the SQL Timed Loop Demo notebook (a ~60-second query loop for testing).
While it runs, resize the active compute UP — show running queries are not interrupted.
View the increased cluster/node count live in the UI.
Resize DOWN and watch the cluster/node count drop in real time.
objects.outcome: Warehouse resizes live; running queries aren't interrupted; scale-down reclaims the clusters.
notes: On serverless, compute size is auto-managed — reframe as "the platform handles this for you" rather than a manual resize.

objects.title: Auto-scaling configuration
objects.surface: SQL Warehouses UI / CLI + load notebook
objects.proves: The platform automatically adds clusters when query concurrency causes queuing, and removes them when idle.
objects.setup: A classic/pro SQL warehouse with min/max clusters > 1. Autoscaling is triggered by QUEUED concurrent queries — not by one big query.
steps: Open the SQL warehouse (Serverless Starter Warehouse) in one tab.
Open and execute the PA_14_AUTO_SCALE_UP_DOWN notebook (concurrent load).
Watch the warehouse scale from 1 to 3 clusters while the notebook runs.
After ~2-3 minutes idle, watch the clusters scale back down.
objects.outcome: Cluster count rises under concurrent load and falls when idle; scaling events are logged. Queuing shows as waiting_at_capacity_duration_ms.
notes: Autoscaling is horizontal (adds clusters), triggered by queued queries. A single heavy query never queues, so it never triggers scale-up — you need concurrency.

objects.title: Compute isolation — workload separation
objects.proves: Different workloads (pipelines, analyst queries, notebooks) run on separate compute so a heavy job on one can't starve another.
objects.setup: Two warehouses (or serverless job compute + a SQL warehouse). Jobs/queries pinned to a specific warehouse_id.
steps: This is a guided conversation on how Databricks compute isolation works — separate warehouses / serverless job compute per workload class, so a heavy analyst query can't starve a production pipeline.
objects.outcome: Two workloads on two warehouses run without interfering; assignments are visible.
notes: The POC already models this — foundation jobs run on serverless, analytics on the SQL warehouse.

objects.title: Pause & resume compute
objects.proves: Compute can be paused during an idle window and resumed on demand without data loss or reconfiguration.
objects.setup: A classic/pro SQL warehouse (stop/start). Serverless scales to zero automatically as its form of pause.
steps: Stop the warehouse if it's running.
Execute any query — show the warehouse/cluster starts automatically on demand.
Highlight the idle-timeout setting on the warehouse and discuss serverless idle behavior.
objects.outcome: Warehouse stops and starts cleanly; a query after resume runs without reconfiguration.
notes: Serverless: show the auto-stop (idle timeout) + on-demand cold start instead of manual stop/start.

objects.title: Capacity dashboard & utilization monitoring
objects.proves: A single dashboard showing current compute utilization, historical usage trends, queue depth, and throttling events — so an admin can spot peak vs. underutilized windows. This is the one built item in PA-E.
objects.setup: Deployed with the bundle: [princeton_poc] PA-17 Capacity & Utilization (ACTIVE). Reads system.query.history — any query activity populates it.
steps: Open the dashboard [princeton_poc] PA-17 Capacity & Utilization (Dashboards → search PA-17).
Read the KPIs (total queries, avg + p95 duration, throttled count) and the hourly volume line — call out a peak hour vs. an idle window.
Show the Throttled Queries KPI + per-user table — the RFP's queue-depth / throttling signal.
To make throttling non-zero, run the PA-14 load notebook first, then refresh.
objects.outcome: Dashboard ACTIVE; shows query volume + latency trend, per-user load, performance-tier split, and the queue/throttle metric; admin identifies peak vs idle windows.
notes: The RFP's "queue depth / throttling" maps to waiting_at_capacity_duration_ms — a native signal, no custom instrumentation.
Distinct from E9 (Workload Monitoring), which tracks job/pipeline RUNS; PA-17 tracks warehouse UTILIZATION.

objects.title: Workload prioritization & queuing
objects.proves: High-priority workloads aren't delayed by lower-priority activity during contention.
objects.setup: A dedicated higher-capacity warehouse for priority/SLA workloads; priority jobs pinned to it via warehouse_id.
steps: This is a guided conversation on workload prioritization — a dedicated higher-capacity warehouse for priority/SLA workloads; prioritization is warehouse-level, not per-query.
objects.outcome: Priority workload completes ahead of lower-priority load during contention.
notes: Honest framing: Databricks doesn't expose per-query priority in standard SQL — prioritization is warehouse-level. Note as a partial/workaround in the vendor response if Princeton expects per-query priority.

objects.title: Spend dashboard — overall platform cost

On Usage Overview, show total spend over time and the product/SKU breakdown (compute vs storage vs egress are distinct SKUs).
Export via the dashboard ⋯ menu (CSV/PDF).
objects.outcome: Spend trend + cost-driver breakdown over the selected period; exportable.
notes: Verify compute/storage/transfer appear as separate SKUs when demoing.

Pick a tag key (e.g. department / cost_center).
Show cost per tag value.
objects.outcome: Cost attributed per department/team/user tag.

objects.title: Cost distribution by pipeline or workload

Set a period, amount, optional filters (workspace/tag), and alert email(s).
Save — show it tracking actual vs threshold; alerts fire as spend approaches the limit.
objects.outcome: A budget with an alert threshold; notification includes current + projected spend vs. the limit.

objects.title: Spend forecasting
objects.proves: Project future platform cost from current usage, ≥30-day horizon.
objects.setup: Usage Dashboard forecast dataset uses AI_FORECAST() with a 90% confidence band.
steps: Open the Usage Dashboard forecast view.
Show the forecast line + confidence band projecting ≥30 days out.
objects.outcome: A ≥30-day spend forecast with a 90% confidence interval.
notes: Forecast accuracy improves with several months of history.

objects.title: Query & job cost estimation
objects.proves: A pre-run resource/cost estimate that aligns with post-run actuals. Honest partial — Databricks is primarily post-run actuals; EXPLAIN COST gives the native pre-run estimate.
objects.setup: Native EXPLAIN COST + Query Profile + system.billing.usage. No build.
steps: Run EXPLAIN COST <a heavy query> in the SQL editor — show estimated statistics (rows/sizes) per plan node BEFORE execution.
Execute the query → open Query Profile → show actual rows/time/memory align with the estimate.
Look the query up in system.billing.usage → show actual $ cost.
objects.outcome: EXPLAIN COST gives a pre-run estimate; Query Profile + billing confirm actuals align. Framed Partial in the vendor response.
notes: No native per-query "$X" preview. For forward workload planning, Lakemeter OSS (Databricks Labs app) gives pre-run workload estimates — noted as an option, not deployed.

objects.title: Cost optimization recommendations

Ask: "What is our total spend in the last 30 days broken down by product?"
Ask: "Which warehouses look idle or underutilized, and what could we save?"

objects.outcome: Genie answers each in natural language with correct SQL over the billing/compute system tables, and flags at least one optimization with an estimated $ figure. (Verified: spend by product returned SQL $8.18, JOBS $1.04, ...)

Honest framing: conversational analysis, analyst-initiated (AI-mediated), not a fully-automated recommendation engine.
